title: 3-Read Friday #96: Visualisers, Instructional Coaching, and Regularities
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #96 curates three posts on classroom practice and instructional theory. Anna Sutton makes the case for the visualiser as an under-appreciated companion to mini-whiteboards, arguing it reduces cognitive load and enacts Rosenshine's modelling principles by showing pupils exactly what success looks like in the context where they will produce it. Adam Boxer takes a critical look at instructional coaching, agreeing it has a strong evidence base while cataloguing the psychological, definitional, financial, and practical barriers that schools underestimate when trying to implement it well. Becky Allen reviews Kris Boulton's work and argues that cognitive science and instructional theory usefully constrain what good teaching can look like, but cannot substitute for the granular, concept-by-concept work of figuring out how to teach any one specific idea well. Barton frames all three as reminders that good classroom tools and good theory both still require careful, deliberate craft to translate into practice.
points: Treat the visualiser as a distinct tool from mini-whiteboards: it reduces cognitive load and models success directly in the context pupils will work in, not just as a generic display device.
Instructional coaching's strong evidence base does not guarantee effective implementation -- psychological, definitional, financial, and practical barriers routinely undermine it in real schools.

Cognitive science and instructional theory set boundaries on what good teaching can be, but they do not replace the granular, concept-specific design work of figuring out how to teach one particular idea well.
Barton's selections this week share a theme: good tools and good theory both demand disciplined, detail-level craft rather than being treated as plug-and-play solutions.
